lessons.title: The turning sky

steps.headline: Earth's spin makes the sky turn about two fixed points, the celestial poles.

lead.text: Extend Earth's axis into space and it meets the sky at two fixed spots. Every star seems to wheel around them. On the equator the raised pole sits on the horizon. At the North Pole it is straight overhead.
Between the equator and the North Pole, the raised pole climbs steadily. Amsterdam lies at 52° N.

reveal.text: Whatever you guessed, the rule is simple: the pole stands as many degrees up as your latitude. Polaris lies close to it, which is how sailors read their latitude.

steps.headline: How far does a star turn in 4 hours?

workedSteps.text: The sky turns steadily, the same angle every hour.
Each hour adds the same 15°, so multiply the rate by the hours.
Calculate.

lead.text: The same steady turning applies on any night. Only the length of the watch changes.

reveal.text: Six hours is a quarter of a full circle. A star on the celestial equator rises in the east and has reached the meridian six hours later.

steps.headline: Declination is a star's latitude on the sky, and a star that never sets is circumpolar.

lead.text: Declination, δ, measures a star north (+) or south (−) of the celestial equator. It is +90° at the north celestial pole and 0° on the equator. A star whose whole daily circle stays above your horizon never sets. We call it circumpolar.
The lowest point of a star's circle lies 90° − δ below the pole. The pole stands φ above your horizon. The star never sets if that lowest point is still above the horizon.

reveal.text: You found the limit. From 52° N every star north of declination +38° is circumpolar; from 10° N only stars beyond +80° are.

lead.text: Each star climbs highest as it crosses the meridian, the north–south line through the zenith. Its altitude then is 90° − |φ − δ|. Southern latitudes and declinations take negative signs.

reveal.text: A star at +20° seen from 52° N peaks 58° up in the south. The same rule works in the southern hemisphere.

lessons.orientation: Use latitude and declination to predict where a star climbs, and whether it ever sets.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Film the night sky for a whole day and every star sweeps out a circle, ending where it began. Assume the turning is steady and a full turn is 360°.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict how high the sky's pole stands and whether a star ever sets from where you are.

recap.keyIdea: Earth's steady spin turns the sky 15° an hour about a celestial pole that stands as high as your latitude. A star never sets if its declination is above 90° − φ.

blocks.text: You found that the sky turns 15° an hour, so 90° in 6 hours. From 52° N the pole stands 52° up and every star north of +38° is circumpolar. A star at +20° peaks at 58°.

recap.nextHook: The sky turns once a day. Why does the Sun's path change over the year?

lessons.title: Why the seasons change

steps.headline: Earth's tilt swings the Sun's declination between +23.4° and −23.4° through the year.

lead.text: Earth's axis is tilted 23.4° from upright to its orbit and always points the same way in space. Around the June solstice, 21 June, the northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun. Around the December solstice, 21 December, it leans away.
The noon Sun stands at 90° − |φ − δ|, the rule you used for stars. In June the Sun's declination δ is the tilt, +23.4°. London lies at 51.5° N.

reveal.text: You used the star rule on the Sun, and it works unchanged. The Sun's declination is just another declination, and in June it puts the noon Sun high over London.

steps.headline: Find the noon Sun's altitude at 35° N on the June solstice.

workedSteps.text: Around 21 June the Sun's declination equals the tilt.
Find the gap between latitude and declination.
Take the gap away from 90°.

lead.text: Now the other solstice. The northern hemisphere leans away from the Sun, so the declination changes sign.

reveal.text: The noon Sun in London climbs far lower in December than in June. The difference is the tilt, not the distance.

steps.headline: A low Sun spreads the same sunlight over more ground, and short days give it less time.

lead.text: A beam arriving at altitude h covers 1/sin h times the ground it covers from overhead. The lower the Sun, the thinner the sunlight. London's daylight lasts about 7.6 hours in December and 16.4 in June.
At the March and September equinoxes the Sun sits on the celestial equator, declination 0°. Day and night last close to 12 hours everywhere.

reveal.text: From 40° N the equinox Sun reaches 50°; from the equator it passes straight overhead.

lead.text: Suppose Earth had no tilt. Distance plays little part in real seasons: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, and its distance varies by only about 3%.

reveal.text: With no tilt the Sun's declination would stay at 0°, and London's noon Sun would sit at the same height all year. The seasons come from the tilt.

lessons.orientation: Explain the seasons from Earth's tilt and calculate the noon height of the Sun.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Each year the spot where the noon Sun is directly overhead drifts from the Tropic of Cancer, 23.4° N, in June to the Tropic of Capricorn, 23.4° S, in December.

intro.promise: By the end you'll explain why noon sunlight is high in summer and low in winter, using Earth's tilt.

recap.keyIdea: Earth's tilt swings the Sun's declination between +23.4° and −23.4°. That changes the noon Sun's height and the day's length. Distance plays almost no part.

blocks.text: You found London's noon Sun at 61.9° in June and 15.1° in December. With no tilt it would stay at 38.5° all year.

recap.nextHook: The Sun's path repeats each year. What of the Moon's monthly cycle of phases and eclipses?

lessons.title: Phases and eclipses

steps.headline: The Moon's phase is how much of its lit half faces us, and the Sun–Moon angle sets it.

lead.text: Sunlight always lights half the Moon. The angle θ between Sun and Moon, seen from Earth, decides how much of that half faces us. At θ = 0° none of it does: new moon. At θ = 180° all of it does: full moon.
Between new moon and full moon, θ grows from 0° to 180°. Think of the moment exactly halfway between them.

reveal.text: Half the disc. The lit fraction is (1 − cos θ)/2, which is one half at θ = 90°. That is first quarter: a “half moon” shows half the disc.

steps.headline: What percentage of the disc is lit when θ = 150°?

workedSteps.text: Use lit fraction = (1 − cos θ)/2.
The cosine of 150° is negative.
Subtracting a negative adds.
Convert to a percentage.

steps.headline: The phases repeat every 29.53 days, the synodic month.

lead.text: From one new moon to the next takes 29.53 days. In that time the Moon gains one full turn, 360°, on the Sun, at a steady rate. Each phase comes round again at the same point of the cycle.
The Moon gains a full turn on the Sun in one synodic month. Treat the gain as steady.

reveal.text: This daily gain is why the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each night: 12.2° of extra turning takes the sky about 49 minutes.

lead.text: The Moon's orbit is tilted 5.1° to the ecliptic, the plane of Earth's orbit. Most months the Moon passes above or below the line through the Sun and Earth. A lunar eclipse needs the Moon inside Earth's shadow.

reveal.text: Earth's shadow points away from the Sun, so the Moon must be on the far side of Earth. Even then it must lie within about 1° of the ecliptic in this model, so most full moons miss.

lead.text: For small angles, angular size in radians is diameter ÷ distance; multiply by 57.3 for degrees. Seen from Earth the Sun spans 0.53°. A total solar eclipse needs the new moon to cover it.

reveal.text: The Moon spans 0.52°, almost exactly the Sun's 0.53°. That match is why a new moon on the ecliptic just covers the Sun's bright disc.

lessons.orientation: Relate the Moon's phase to the Sun–Earth–Moon angle and explain when eclipses happen.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The Moon passes from new moon to full moon and back to new moon in about 30 days.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a Moon phase as an angle and say why eclipses are rarer than new and full moons.

recap.keyIdea: The Moon's phase is set by the Sun–Earth–Moon angle and repeats every 29.53 days. Eclipses need an exact alignment, which the 5.1° tilt of the Moon's orbit makes rare.

blocks.text: You found that half the disc is lit at 90°, that the Moon gains 12.2° a day on the Sun, and that it spans 0.52° against the Sun's 0.53°.

recap.nextHook: Phases come from simple geometry. What geometry governs how fast a planet moves round the Sun?

lessons.title: Kepler's laws

steps.headline: Each planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.

lead.text: An ellipse is a stretched circle. Half its longest diameter is the semi-major axis, a. The eccentricity, e, says how stretched it is: 0 is a circle. The closest point to the Sun is perihelion and the farthest is aphelion.
The Sun sits a distance a × e from the centre of the ellipse, towards one end. Earth's e is 0.017, so its distance from the Sun changes by only about 3%.

reveal.text: Perihelion is a − a × e, which is a(1 − e). Whatever you guessed, the stretch e pulls the closest point in from a by the fraction e.

steps.headline: Find the aphelion distance when a = 3 AU and e = 0.5.

workedSteps.text: The far end is the centre-to-Sun gap, a × e, beyond a.
Put in the numbers.
Calculate.

steps.headline: A planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, so it moves fastest at perihelion.

lead.text: This is Kepler's second law. The line from Sun to planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Near the Sun that line is short, so the planet must cover a longer arc in the same time. It speeds up.
At the two ends of the long axis, the speeds are in the inverse ratio of the distances from the Sun.

reveal.text: The planet is four times faster at perihelion than at aphelion. Equal areas in equal times forces the speed to change this much.

lead.text: Kepler's third law: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. With P in years and a in AU around the Sun, P² = a³. The period depends only on a, not on e.

reveal.text: P² = 64, so P = 8: a bigger orbit takes much longer than its size alone suggests, because the planet also moves slower.

lead.text: Around a star of M solar masses the law becomes P² = a³ ÷ M. A stronger pull needs a faster orbit to keep from falling inward.

reveal.text: A heavier star shortens the period: the same orbit size is covered more quickly because the pull is stronger.

lessons.orientation: Describe an orbit by its size and shape, and link its period to its semi-major axis.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A comet's orbit is a long oval. The Sun sits inside it, on the line through the oval's two ends. At its closest the comet is 1 AU from the Sun, and at its farthest 9 AU.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find an orbit's closest and farthest points and use its size to work out its period.

recap.keyIdea: A planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, fastest at perihelion. Its period in years and semi-major axis in AU satisfy P² = a³.

blocks.text: You found that an orbit running from 1 AU to 9 AU has a long axis of 10 AU, and that an asteroid with a = 2 AU and e = 0.6 moves four times faster at perihelion. A 4 AU orbit takes 8 years.

recap.nextHook: Kepler described the orbits without explaining them. What force makes a planet follow them?

lessons.title: Newton's gravitation

steps.headline: Every pair of masses attracts with a force F = GMm/r², which weakens as the square of the separation.

lead.text: M and m are the two masses and r is the distance between them. G, the gravitational constant, is a fixed number: 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². A bigger mass strengthens the pull. A bigger separation weakens it, by the square.
The arrows in the drawing share one scale, so you can watch the force shrink as the bodies move apart.

reveal.text: Double the separation and the force falls to a quarter; triple it and it falls to a ninth. That is what the 1/r² in the law does.

steps.headline: By what factor does the force change when r is halved and one mass is doubled?

workedSteps.text: Halving r multiplies the force by the square of 2.
Doubling one mass multiplies the force by 2.
Each change acts on its own, so the factors multiply.

lead.text: Here the separation stays fixed. Only the masses change.

reveal.text: The force depends on the product of the masses. Doubling one and tripling the other multiplies the pull by both factors.

steps.headline: Divide the force by the falling object's own mass and the acceleration g = GM/r² is left.

lead.text: The force on a mass m is GMm/r². Divide by m and the m cancels: g = GM/r². Here M is the mass of the body doing the pulling. Every falling object at that place gets the same acceleration, whatever its own mass.
Use SI units throughout. GM is in m³/s², so convert the radius from kilometres to metres before you square it.

reveal.text: That 9.82 m/s² is how fast any object gains speed near Earth's surface. The same formula gives the Moon's gravity from its own GM and radius.

lead.text: The field g = GM/r² applies to any planet. Take a planet with Earth's mass but twice Earth's radius.

reveal.text: Doubling r with the mass fixed divides g by four. The same inverse-square rule governs a planet's surface and a spacecraft's height.

lessons.orientation: Use the inverse-square law of gravity to compare forces and compute surface gravity.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Earth and the Moon tug on each other across 384,000 km. Earth has 81 times the Moon's mass.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use F = GMm/r² to say how gravity changes with distance and mass, and to find g.

recap.keyIdea: Gravity pulls every pair of masses with F = GMm/r². The force falls as the square of the separation, and g = GM/r² is the same for every falling object.

blocks.text: You found that Earth and the Moon pull on each other equally, and that tripling the separation cuts the pull to a ninth. At Earth's surface g is 9.82 m/s².

recap.nextHook: One law covers the falling apple and the Moon. How fast must something go to stay in orbit, or to leave?

lessons.title: Orbits, escape and tides

steps.headline: An orbit is a fall that keeps missing, at the circular speed v = √(GM/r).

lead.text: At distance r from the centre of a body, one speed curves the path away exactly as fast as gravity pulls inward: v = √(GM/r). Slower, the path meets the ground. Faster, it stretches into an ellipse.

steps.headline: Find the circular speed at the Moon's distance, 384,400 km from Earth's centre.

workedSteps.text: Write r in metres.
Divide GM by r.
Take the square root.

lead.text: Measure r from Earth's centre, not from the ground. Work in metres, as in the example.

reveal.text: Almost 8 km/s: the same speed as in the opening puzzle, now from the formula. Skim Earth's surface at that speed and the ground curves away as fast as you fall.

steps.headline: Escape speed is √2 times the circular speed at the same distance.

lead.text: Launch fast enough and the path opens out and never returns. The escape speed is v = √(2GM/r). Its ratio to the circular speed is always the same, about 1.41, wherever you are.
From the surface, r is Earth's radius. The formula is the same as before, with a 2 under the root.

reveal.text: About 11 km/s, √2 times the speed that merely skims the surface. Air resistance is ignored.

lead.text: The same formula works for planets around the Sun. Use the Sun's GM and Earth's distance from the Sun.

reveal.text: 29.8 km/s matches NASA's measured mean of 29.78 km/s. One formula serves satellites and planets.

lead.text: The Moon pulls Earth's near ocean harder than Earth's centre, and the centre harder than the far ocean. That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges: two high tides a day. The stretch falls as the cube of distance.

reveal.text: A difference in pull falls faster than the pull itself, so halving the distance multiplies the tide by 8. The Sun's tide is 0.46 of the Moon's. When the two line up at new and full moon they add, giving spring tides.

cases.label: Moon today, Sun at right angles

lessons.orientation: Compute circular and escape speeds and explain tides as a difference in pull.

blocks.text: Fire a cannonball horizontally and it falls 5 m in the first second. Earth's surface curves away by 5 m over every 8 km along a straight line. Ignore the air.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the speeds for orbiting and escaping, and say why tides depend on distance cubed.

recap.keyIdea: Gravity sets the speed that keeps a circular orbit, √(GM/r), and the escape speed, √2 times larger. Tides come from a difference in pull, which falls as 1/d³.

blocks.text: You found that skimming Earth takes about 8 km/s, that a satellite 400 km up needs 7.67 km/s, and that escaping Earth takes 11.19 km/s. Halving the Moon's distance would multiply its tides by 8.

lessons.title: Brightness and distance

steps.headline: A star's flux is its luminosity spread over a sphere: F = L/(4πd²).

lead.text: A star's luminosity, L, is its total power output. At distance d that power spreads over a sphere of area 4πd². The power arriving on each square metre is the flux, F.
The same light covers a bigger sphere the farther you go. The drawing shows the Sun's light at three distances.

reveal.text: At twice the distance the same light covers four times the area, so the flux falls to a quarter. At three times it falls to a ninth, just as the torch did.

steps.headline: How much solar flux reaches Jupiter, 5 AU from the Sun?

workedSteps.text: Write the distance in metres.
Find the area of the sphere the light has spread over.
Divide the luminosity by that area.

lead.text: Use SI units, so the distance is in metres. The Sun's luminosity is 3.828 × 10²⁶ W.

reveal.text: About 1,361 W on every square metre facing the Sun, above the atmosphere. That figure is called the solar constant.

steps.headline: A star's yearly shift against the distant stars gives its distance: d = 1/p parsecs.

lead.text: As Earth swings round the Sun, a nearby star shifts against far more distant stars. Half that seasonal shift is the parallax, p. A star with p = 1 arcsecond is 1 parsec away, by definition. In general d = 1/p, with p in arcseconds.
A larger shift means a nearer star. Use d = 1/p.

reveal.text: You turned a shift of less than one arcsecond into a distance of 1.30 pc, about 4.25 light-years.

lead.text: Apparent brightness alone cannot separate a powerful distant star from a feeble nearby one. Flux is L/(4πd²), so a change in luminosity and a change in distance both alter it.

reveal.text: Equal flux needs L/d² to match, so d grows as the square root of L. Once parallax gives d, the measured flux gives L = 4πd²F.

lessons.orientation: Apply the inverse-square law to starlight and measure distance by parallax.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A torch shines a cone of light onto a wall 1 m away and lights a circle. Now you step back to 3 m. The cone is the same, so the circle grows.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a star's distance from its parallax and its luminosity from its brightness.

recap.keyIdea: A star's flux is its luminosity spread over a sphere, F = L/(4πd²). Parallax gives the distance, and with the distance the flux gives the luminosity.

blocks.text: You found that stepping back from 1 m to 3 m spreads a torch's light over 9 times the area, and that the Sun delivers 1,361 W/m² at Earth. Proxima Centauri is 1.30 pc away.

recap.nextHook: Distance and brightness give a star's luminosity. What do its colour and motion tell us?

lessons.title: Temperature, colour and motion

steps.headline: A hotter star peaks at a shorter wavelength: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K ÷ T.

lead.text: A star radiates roughly like a blackbody, whose spectrum has a single peak. Wien's law gives the peak wavelength from the surface temperature T in kelvin. Hotter means a shorter peak, so bluer light.

steps.headline: Find the peak wavelength of a star with a surface temperature of 9,000 K.

workedSteps.text: Divide Wien's constant by the temperature.
Convert metres to nanometres by multiplying by 10⁹.
Compare with visible light, which runs from about 400 to 700 nm.

lead.text: Same law, with the Sun's surface temperature. Give the peak in nanometres.

reveal.text: The Sun's peak is in the blue-green, but it emits right across the visible range, so it looks white.

lead.text: Run Wien's law backwards to take a star's temperature from a distance: T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K ÷ λmax. Write λmax in metres.

reveal.text: A peak at 290 nm lies in the ultraviolet. Hot stars like Vega, near 10,000 K, look blue-white.

steps.headline: A receding source's light shifts to longer wavelengths, by v = cΔλ/λ.

lead.text: Laboratory wavelengths are fixed. A source moving away stretches its waves: a redshift. One approaching squeezes them: a blueshift. For speeds well below light's, the speed along the line of sight is v = cΔλ/λ.
Δλ is the observed wavelength minus the laboratory one. Positive means receding.

reveal.text: A shift of about 1% of the wavelength means a speed of about 1% of c. That is how astronomers measure speeds of stars and galaxies they will never visit.

lead.text: Stars in our galaxy move at tens to hundreds of kilometres per second, so their shifts are tiny. An approaching source has a negative radial velocity.

reveal.text: The line moves 0.25 nm towards the blue. Only motion along the line of sight shows up: sideways motion produces no first-order shift.

lessons.orientation: Read a star's temperature from its colour and its motion from shifted spectral lines.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Atoms emit light at fixed wavelengths. When the source moves away from you, the waves it sends are stretched.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a star's temperature from its colour and its speed from the shift in its spectral lines.

recap.keyIdea: A star's colour gives its temperature through Wien's law, and the shift of its spectral lines gives its speed along our line of sight, v = cΔλ/λ.

blocks.text: You found that the Sun peaks at 502 nm, that a 290 nm peak means about 10,000 K, and that a 1% stretch of a line means a speed of 1% of light's.

recap.nextHook: Temperature and brightness are two measurements of a star. What happens when you plot one against the other?

lessons.title: The H–R diagram

steps.headline: A star's luminosity grows with its surface area and, much faster, with its temperature.

lead.text: Each square metre of surface emits power proportional to T⁴, and the surface area is 4πR². In solar units, with R in solar radii and T measured against the Sun's 5,772 K, this becomes L = R²(T/T☉)⁴.

steps.headline: Find the luminosity of a star with R = 2 R☉ and T = 1.5 T☉.

workedSteps.text: Write the law in solar units.
Work out each factor.
Multiply them.

lead.text: The radius stays at the Sun's, so R² = 1. Only the temperature changes.

reveal.text: Doubling the temperature multiplies the luminosity by 2⁴, so temperature is a far stronger lever than radius.

steps.headline: The H–R diagram plots luminosity against temperature, and stars fall into groups.

lead.text: Temperature runs backwards, with the hottest stars on the left. Most stars lie on the main sequence, a diagonal band. Up and to the right sit cool stars so luminous they must be enormous: giants and supergiants. Down on the left are hot, dim white dwarfs.
Up and to the right sit cool stars so luminous they must be enormous. Work out how luminous one is.

reveal.text: A cool surface alone would make the star dim. Only an enormous radius gives it tens of thousands of times the Sun's output.

lead.text: Down in the lower left lie white dwarfs: hot but dim, so they must be tiny. Lines of constant radius slant across the diagram.

reveal.text: A star the size of Earth, yet hotter than the Sun, gives out only a few hundredths of the Sun's power.

lead.text: On the diagram, stars of equal temperature sit in a vertical line. Moving up that line raises the luminosity but not the power per square metre.

reveal.text: Equal temperature means equal power per square metre, so extra luminosity has to come from extra surface area. Height on the diagram at fixed temperature measures size.

lessons.orientation: Relate luminosity, radius and temperature, and read a star's size from its place on the diagram.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two stars have the same surface temperature, so each square metre of surface shines equally. Star A has twice the radius of star B.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a star's luminosity from its radius and temperature, and read its type from the H–R diagram.

recap.keyIdea: A star's luminosity is L = R²(T/T☉)⁴: temperature matters most, then radius. On the H–R diagram that sorts stars into the main sequence, giants and white dwarfs.

blocks.text: You found that doubling the radius quadruples the light at the same temperature, that doubling the temperature multiplies it by 16, and that a cool supergiant gives about 87,000 L☉.

recap.nextHook: A star's place on the diagram depends on its mass. How does mass set how long a star lives?

lessons.title: How mass sets a star's life

steps.headline: A star's life is its fuel divided by its burn rate, and mass raises the burn rate faster than the fuel.

lead.text: On the main sequence a star fuses hydrogen in its core. Fuel grows roughly in proportion to the mass M. The burn rate, the luminosity, grows roughly as M³·⁵. Lifetime is fuel ÷ burn rate, so t ∝ M⁻²·⁵. The Sun lasts about 10 billion years.

steps.headline: Find the main-sequence lifetime of a 2 M☉ star.

workedSteps.text: Work out the power of the mass.
Divide the Sun's lifetime by it.
Calculate.

lead.text: Same rule, a heavier star. Give the answer in millions of years.

reveal.text: A star four times the Sun's mass lasts only about 3% as long. More fuel does not make up for a much faster burn.

lead.text: Turn the rule round. Divide the lifetime by 10 billion years to get M⁻²·⁵, then raise that number to the power −1/2.5 to get M.

reveal.text: A star that lasts only 10 million years is about 16 times the Sun's mass. Short lives mean heavy stars.

lead.text: The rule L ∝ M³·⁵ is a fit to measured main-sequence stars, good to about a factor of two. Split the power as 2³ × 2⁰·⁵.

reveal.text: A 10 M☉ star shines at about 3,200 L☉. Mass fixes where a main-sequence star sits on the H–R diagram.

lead.text: When core hydrogen runs out, the core contracts and the outer layers swell into a giant. OpenStax's table of end states: below about 10 M☉ a white dwarf, from about 10 to 40 M☉ a neutron star, above that a black hole.

reveal.text: A star's initial mass decides its remnant. A 15 M☉ star sits in the middle band: its core collapses in a supernova but stops short of a black hole.

lessons.title: Galaxies and Hubble's law

steps.headline: Galaxies recede at a speed proportional to their distance: Hubble's law, v = H₀d.

lead.text: Galaxy spectra are redshifted, and the redshift grows with distance. Hubble's law gives the recession speed as v = H₀d. H₀ is the Hubble constant, about 70 km/s per megaparsec (Mpc). One Mpc is 3.26 million light-years.
Light takes time to arrive. A distance of 1 Mpc is 3.26 million light-years, so light from it has travelled for 3.26 million years.

reveal.text: You were looking at Andromeda as it was millions of years ago. The farther away a galaxy is, the older the light we see.

steps.headline: How fast does a galaxy 30 Mpc away recede, with H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc?

workedSteps.text: Use Hubble's law.
Put in the numbers. The Mpc cancels.
Calculate.

lead.text: Same law, a farther galaxy. Remember H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc.

reveal.text: Twice the distance gives twice the speed. At 200 Mpc the same law gives double what you just found.

steps.headline: Expansion has no centre, and running the law backwards turns a speed into a distance.

lead.text: Stretch the grid evenly and every gap grows by the same factor. A galaxy twice as far gains twice as much, so observers in any galaxy see v proportional to d. Reversing the law gives d = v ÷ H₀.
A recession speed gives a distance by d = v ÷ H₀, with H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc.

reveal.text: A faster galaxy is a farther one: you have turned a measured speed into a distance.

lead.text: Different methods give H₀ between about 67 and 73 km/s per Mpc, a disagreement called the Hubble tension. Distances found from velocities inherit that uncertainty.

reveal.text: The two values predict speeds that differ by the gap in H₀ times the distance. A small disagreement in H₀ grows with distance.

lessons.orientation: Picture the scale of the universe and use Hubble's law to link velocity and distance.

blocks.text: Dots A, B and C lie in a line on a rubber sheet. B is 10 cm from A and C is 20 cm from A. The sheet is stretched evenly until every gap has doubled.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn a galaxy's redshift into a distance with Hubble's law and say why expansion has no centre.

recap.keyIdea: Galaxies recede at v = H₀d, so a redshift gives a distance. Uniform expansion looks the same from every galaxy, so it has no centre.

blocks.text: You found that on a stretching sheet the longer gap gains twice as much, that a galaxy 100 Mpc away recedes at 7,000 km/s, and that one receding at 14,000 km/s is 200 Mpc away.

recap.nextHook: If everything is moving apart, it was once together. How long ago, and what afterglow would it leave?

lessons.title: The age and afterglow of the Big Bang

steps.headline: Run the expansion backwards and every galaxy set off 1/H₀ ago.

lead.text: If each galaxy had always receded at its present speed, one at distance d set off a time d ÷ v ago. Since v = H₀d, the d cancels: the time is 1/H₀, the same for every galaxy. This is the expansion age.

steps.headline: Find 1/H₀ in billions of years for H₀ = 60 km/s per Mpc.

workedSteps.text: Write 1 Mpc in kilometres, so the kilometres cancel.
Divide to get seconds.
Divide by the seconds in a billion years.

lead.text: Same method with H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc. Use 1 Mpc = 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km and 1 billion years = 3.156 × 10¹⁶ s.

reveal.text: About 14 billion years. Careful modelling of the changing expansion gives 13.8 billion years, so this simple estimate is close.

steps.headline: A hot, dense early universe leaves a cold, uniform glow: the cosmic microwave background.

lead.text: In 1965 Penzias and Wilson found faint microwave radiation arriving equally from every direction. Its spectrum is an almost perfect blackbody at 2.725 K, just what a universe that was once hot and dense should leave behind.
Wien's law applies as before: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K ÷ T. Give the answer in millimetres.

reveal.text: A peak near a millimetre lies in the microwave range, which is how the background got its name.

lead.text: About 380,000 years after the Big Bang the universe had cooled to about 3,000 K, cool enough for electrons to join nuclei into neutral atoms. Light then travelled freely. Since then expansion has stretched every wavelength, and the temperature has fallen in step.

reveal.text: Every wavelength has grown about a thousand-fold. Glow that left as visible and infrared light now arrives as microwaves.

lead.text: The age estimate is inversely proportional to H₀. Use 1/H₀ = 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀, which has the unit conversion built in.

reveal.text: A smaller H₀ means slower expansion, so the galaxies took longer to get where they are. Stars older than 1/H₀ would be a contradiction.

lessons.orientation: Estimate the age of the universe from H₀ and read its early heat in the microwave background.

questions.prompt: From latitude 52° N, what is the altitude of the north celestial pole, in degrees?
hints: The pole's altitude is tied to where you stand on Earth.
At the equator the pole is on the horizon; at the North Pole it is overhead.
Altitude of the pole equals the observer's latitude.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The raised celestial pole stands at an altitude equal to the latitude: 52°.

questions.onCorrect: 52°. The raised pole stands as high above the horizon as your latitude.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the pole's height at the North Pole, latitude 90°. Amsterdam is much further south.
That measures the angle the other way, from the pole to the zenith. The pole's height is the latitude itself.

questions.prompt: The sky turns about 15° an hour. Through what angle, in degrees, does a star move around its daily circle in 6 hours?
hints: The rate is constant through the night.
Multiply the rate by the time.
Calculate 15 × 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 15° per hour × 6 h = 90°, a quarter of a full circle.

questions.onCorrect: 90°. Steady turning means angle = rate × time, so 6 hours is a quarter of a circle.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the hours to the rate. They are different quantities: multiply them instead.
That divides the rate by the hours. The angle grows with time, so the hours multiply.

questions.prompt: From latitude 52° N, a star is circumpolar when its declination exceeds 90° − φ. What is that smallest declination, in degrees?
hints: The lowest point of the star's circle must stay above the horizon.
The lowest point lies 90° − δ below a pole that is φ high.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: δ > 90° − 52° = 38°. Stars north of +38° never set from 52° N.

questions.onCorrect: 38°. The limit is measured from the pole, so subtract the latitude from 90°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude itself. The limit is measured from the pole, so the latitude has to be taken from 90°.
Only a star exactly at the pole would qualify under that limit. Every star close to it must qualify as well.

questions.prompt: A star of declination +20° crosses the meridian as seen from latitude 52° N. What is its altitude then, in degrees?
hints: The highest altitude comes on the meridian.
Find the difference between latitude and declination, then subtract it from 90°.
questions.onCorrect: 58°. Altitude on the meridian is 90° minus the gap between latitude and declination.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between latitude and declination. The altitude is what is left of 90° after the gap.
That adds latitude and declination. The rule uses the difference between them.

questions.prompt: Seen from latitude 30° N, a star of declination −10° crosses the meridian. Find its altitude in degrees.
hints: A southern declination enters with a minus sign.
The difference φ − δ is 30 − (−10).
Subtract that difference from 90°.
questions.onCorrect: 50°. A southern declination keeps its minus sign, so the gap is 40° and the altitude is 90° minus it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between latitude and declination. Take it away from 90°.
That treats −10° as +10°. A southern declination keeps its sign, which makes the gap larger.

questions.prompt: What single word names a star that never sets as seen from a given latitude?
hints: The star's circle stays around the pole without dipping below the horizon.

acceptedIdeas: circumpolar
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Circumpolar: its whole daily circle stays above the horizon around the celestial pole.

questions.onCorrect: Circumpolar: the whole daily circle stays above the horizon.

misconceptions.feedback: The meridian is a line across the sky, not a kind of star. The word you want describes a star that never sets.

questions.prompt: London lies at 51.5° N. Taking Earth's tilt as 23.4°, find the Sun's noon altitude at the June solstice, in degrees, to one decimal place.
hints: At the June solstice the Sun's declination equals the tilt, north of the equator.
Find 51.5 − 23.4 first, then subtract it from 90.
questions.onCorrect: 61.9°. The June Sun's declination is +23.4°, which narrows the gap to London's latitude.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between latitude and declination. The altitude is what is left of 90° after the gap.
That is the December figure. In June the Sun is north of the equator, so the gap is smaller.

questions.prompt: Find the Sun's noon altitude in London (51.5° N) at the December solstice, with a tilt of 23.4°, to one decimal place.
hints: In December the Sun's declination is south of the equator, so it is negative.
Subtract that sum from 90°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the December solstice δ = −23.4°. Altitude = 90° − |51.5° + 23.4°| = 90° − 74.9° = 15.1°.

questions.onCorrect: 15.1°. In December the Sun's declination is −23.4°, so the gap to London grows and the Sun stays low.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the June figure. In December the declination is negative and the gap grows.
That is the gap between latitude and declination. Take it away from 90°.

questions.prompt: At an equinox the Sun's declination is 0°. Find the noon altitude of the Sun from latitude 40° N, in degrees.
hints: Set δ to zero.
The rule reduces to 90° − φ.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.
questions.onCorrect: 50°. At an equinox δ is 0°, so the noon altitude is simply 90° minus the latitude.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude. Altitude is measured up from the horizon, so take the latitude away from 90°.

questions.prompt: Imagine Earth had no axial tilt. What would the Sun's noon altitude be in London (51.5° N) on every date, in degrees, to one decimal place?
hints: Without tilt the Sun never leaves the celestial equator.
Its declination is zero on every date.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no tilt δ = 0° all year, so the noon altitude is always 90° − 51.5° = 38.5°.

questions.onCorrect: 38.5°. With no tilt δ stays 0°, so the noon Sun never changes height.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude. Take it away from 90° to get the altitude.
That is London's June figure. With no tilt the Sun never leaves the celestial equator.

questions.prompt: At what northern latitude, in degrees, is the noon Sun directly overhead at the June solstice, taking Earth's tilt as 23.4°? Give one decimal place.
hints: Directly overhead means an altitude of 90°.
Set 90° − |φ − δ| equal to 90°.
The latitude must match the Sun's declination on that date.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Overhead means altitude 90°, so |φ − δ| = 0 and φ = δ = 23.4° N, the Tropic of Cancer.

questions.onCorrect: 23.4° N. The Sun is overhead where latitude equals its declination, the Tropic of Cancer in June.

misconceptions.feedback: 90° is the Sun's altitude, not a latitude. The question asks where on Earth that happens.
The equator sees the overhead Sun at the equinoxes. At the June solstice the Sun is north of it.

questions.prompt: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. Why is it winter in the northern hemisphere then?
hints: Compare the two hemispheres: they have opposite seasons at the same distance from the Sun.

acceptedIdeas: The northern hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, so sunlight arrives low and days are short
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Seasons follow the tilt. In January the north leans away from the Sun: a low noon Sun spreads its energy thinly over short days, while the 3% change in distance matters little.

choices.label: The northern hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, so sunlight arrives low and days are short
The Sun gives out less energy in January
Earth's orbit carries it farthest from the Sun in January

questions.onCorrect: Seasons follow the tilt. In January the north leans away, so the Sun is low and the days are short.

misconceptions.feedback: The Sun's output hardly changes through the year. The tilt does the work.
The question says Earth is closest in January. Distance cannot explain winter then.

questions.prompt: When the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 90°, what percentage of the Moon's visible disc is lit?
hints: Use lit fraction = (1 − cos θ)/2.
The cosine of 90° is zero.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Lit fraction = (1 − cos 90°)/2 = (1 − 0)/2, half the disc.

questions.onCorrect: 50%. At θ = 90° half the disc is lit: the quarter phases show half a disc.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole disc, which happens at θ = 180°. Halfway round, the lit half is only partly turned towards us.
That is the lit fraction at θ = 60°. By 90° more of the lit half has turned towards us.

questions.prompt: The synodic month is 29.53 days. How many degrees per day does the Moon gain on the Sun? Give one decimal place.
hints: In one synodic month the Moon gains one full turn on the Sun.
A full turn is 360°.
Divide 360 by the number of days.
questions.onCorrect: 12.2° a day. One full turn spread steadily over the synodic month.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole turn. The question asks how much is gained each day.
That is the number of days. Share the full turn out over them.

questions.prompt: At which phase of the Moon can a lunar eclipse happen? Answer with one word.
hints: Earth's shadow points directly away from the Sun.

acceptedIdeas: full
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Full: Earth must sit between the Sun and the Moon so the Moon can pass through Earth's shadow.

questions.onCorrect: Full: Earth must sit between the Sun and the Moon, so the Moon can enter Earth's shadow.

misconceptions.feedback: At new moon the Moon is between Earth and the Sun. Earth's shadow points away from the Sun, so the Moon would have to be on the far side.

questions.prompt: The Moon is 3,475 km across and 384,400 km away. Find its angular diameter in degrees, to two decimal places, using angle ≈ diameter/distance and 1 radian = 57.3°.
hints: Divide the diameter by the distance to get radians.
Convert radians to degrees with the factor 57.3.
Round the result to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: 0.52°. Angular size is diameter ÷ distance in radians, times 57.3 for degrees.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the angle in radians. Multiply by 57.3 to turn it into degrees.

questions.prompt: How many days after new moon is first quarter, taking the synodic month as 29.53 days? Give two decimal places.
hints: First quarter is a Sun–Earth–Moon angle of 90°.
That is one quarter of the full cycle.
Divide the synodic month by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: First quarter is a quarter of the cycle: 29.53 ÷ 4 = 7.3825, about 7.38 days.

questions.onCorrect: 7.38 days. First quarter is θ = 90°, a quarter of the way round the cycle.

misconceptions.feedback: That is half the cycle, the full moon. First quarter comes a quarter of the way round.
That is three quarters of the cycle: third quarter. First quarter comes earlier.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the Moon's visible disc is lit when the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 120°?
hints: Use (1 − cos θ)/2.
The cosine of 120° is −0.5.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 75%. At θ = 120° the cosine is negative, so more than half the disc is lit.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats cos 120° as +0.5. It is negative, which makes the lit part larger.
That would be θ = 90°. At 120° more of the lit half has turned towards us.

questions.prompt: An asteroid's orbit has semi-major axis 2 AU and eccentricity 0.6. How close does it come to the Sun, in AU?
hints: The Sun sits at a focus, a × e from the centre.
Perihelion distance is a(1 − e).
Calculate 2 × (1 − 0.6).
questions.onCorrect: 0.8 AU. The Sun sits a × e from the centre, so perihelion is a(1 − e).

misconceptions.feedback: That is a × e, the gap between the Sun and the centre. Closest approach is measured from the Sun, so take that gap off a.
That is the far end. The closest point lies on the near side of the Sun.

questions.prompt: For the orbit with a = 2 AU and e = 0.6, the speed at perihelion divided by the speed at aphelion equals the aphelion distance divided by the perihelion distance. Find this ratio.
hints: Aphelion is a(1 + e) and perihelion is a(1 − e).
Work out both distances.
Divide 3.2 by 0.8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Aphelion 3.2 AU ÷ perihelion 0.8 AU = 4. The asteroid moves four times faster at its closest point.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The speeds are in the inverse ratio of the distances, so the closer end is faster.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. The planet is faster at the closer end.
That is the aphelion distance, not a ratio of the two distances.

questions.prompt: An asteroid orbits the Sun with semi-major axis 4 AU. Using P² = a³ (P in years, a in AU), find its period in years.
hints: Cube the semi-major axis.
That gives P².
Take the square root of 64.
questions.onCorrect: 8 years. Cube a to get P², then take the square root.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P². The law gives the square of the period, so take the square root.
That is the square root of a. The law cubes a first.

questions.prompt: A planet orbits a star of 4 solar masses with a = 1 AU. Using P² = a³/M, find its period in years.
hints: Divide a³ by the star's mass in solar masses.
1 cubed is 1.
Take the square root of a quarter.
questions.onCorrect: 0.5 years. A heavier star divides P² by M, so the period shrinks.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P². Take the square root to get the period.
That is the period around a Sun-like star. A heavier star pulls harder and shortens it.

questions.prompt: Jupiter's orbital period is 11.86 years. Using P² = a³, find its semi-major axis in AU, to two decimal places.
hints: Square the period to get a³.
11.86² is about 140.7.
Take the cube root of that.
questions.onCorrect: 5.20 AU. Square the period to get a³, then take the cube root.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a³. Take the cube root to find a.
That is the square root of the period. P² = a³ makes a the cube root of P².

questions.prompt: What name is given to the point of a planet's orbit closest to the Sun?
hints: It begins with the Greek prefix for 'near'.

acceptedIdeas: perihelion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Perihelion, from Greek peri (near) and helios (Sun). The farthest point is aphelion.

questions.onCorrect: Perihelion: peri means near and helios means Sun.

misconceptions.feedback: Aphelion is the farthest point. The closest point has the prefix that means near.

questions.prompt: Two bodies are moved from separation r to 3r. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change? Give three decimal places.
hints: Gravity follows an inverse-square law.
Square the factor by which the distance grew.
Take the reciprocal of 3².
questions.onCorrect: 0.111. Force follows 1/r², so tripling the separation divides the force by nine.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the force as falling in proportion to the distance. Gravity follows the square of it.
That makes the force grow. The force weakens as the bodies move apart.

questions.prompt: At a fixed separation, one mass is doubled and the other tripled. By what factor does the gravitational force change?
hints: The force is proportional to the product of the masses.
Each mass change multiplies the force.
Multiply the two factors.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F ∝ Mm, so the force changes by 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Force is proportional to the product of the masses, so the factors multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the factors. The force depends on the product of the masses, so the factors multiply.

questions.prompt: Earth's GM is 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and its radius is 6,371 km. Find g = GM/R² at the surface, in m/s², to two decimal places.
hints: Convert the radius to metres first.
Square 6.371 × 10⁶ m.
Divide GM by that square.
questions.onCorrect: 9.82 m/s². Surface gravity is GM divided by the radius squared, in metres.

misconceptions.feedback: The radius must be in metres to match GM. In kilometres the answer comes out a million times too large.

questions.prompt: How many times as large as the Moon's pull on Earth is Earth's pull on the Moon?
hints: Think of the pair as a tug of war between two bodies.
Whatever force acts on one body from the other, the other feels a force from it.
Newton's third law pairs the two forces.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both forces equal GMm/r², so the ratio is exactly one: equal and opposite.

questions.onCorrect: 1. The two forces are an equal and opposite pair: GMm/r² is the same whichever body you call M.

misconceptions.feedback: The 81 shows up in how much each body accelerates, not in the size of the pull. Think of the pair as one tug of war.

questions.prompt: Mars has GM = 4.283 × 10¹³ m³/s² and radius 3,390 km. Find its surface gravity in m/s², to two decimal places.
hints: Use g = GM/R² with R in metres.
Square 3.39 × 10⁶.
Divide GM by that square.
questions.onCorrect: 3.73 m/s². The same formula gives each world's surface gravity from its own GM and radius.

misconceptions.feedback: The radius must be in metres to match GM. Kilometres give an answer a million times too large.

questions.prompt: Why do a hammer and a feather dropped together on the Moon land together?
hints: Divide the gravitational force by the falling object's own mass.

acceptedIdeas: The pull on each is proportional to its mass, so the acceleration GM/r² is the same for both
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Force GMm/r² divided by the object's mass m leaves GM/r², the same for any object at that place. With no air there is no drag to separate them.

choices.label: The pull on each is proportional to its mass, so the acceleration GM/r² is the same for both
The Moon's gravity does not act on light objects
Heavier objects are pulled less strongly per kilogram

questions.onCorrect: The mass cancels in GMm/r² ÷ m, leaving GM/r². The acceleration is the same for every object.

misconceptions.feedback: Gravity acts on light and heavy objects alike. The question is what it does to their acceleration.
Divide GMm/r² by m and see whether any of the object's own mass is left.

questions.prompt: Find the circular orbital speed 400 km above Earth, where r = 6,771 km and GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², in km/s, to two decimal places.
hints: Use v = √(GM/r) with r in metres.
Divide GM by 6.771 × 10⁶ m.
Take the square root and convert from m/s to km/s.
questions.onCorrect: 7.67 km/s. Divide GM by r in metres, take the square root, then convert to km/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in metres per second. Divide by 1,000 to give km/s.

questions.prompt: Find the escape speed from Earth's surface, with R = 6,371 km and GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², in km/s, to two decimal places.
hints: Use v = √(2GM/r).
Double GM, then divide by the radius in metres.
Take the square root and convert to km/s.
questions.onCorrect: 11.19 km/s. The escape speed has a 2 under the root, so it exceeds the circular speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the circular speed at the surface. Escape needs more, with the extra 2 under the root.
That is in metres per second. Divide by 1,000 for km/s.

questions.prompt: Using v = √(GM/r) with GM☉ = 1.327 × 10²⁰ m³/s² and r = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, find Earth's orbital speed in km/s, to one decimal place.
hints: This is a circular-orbit speed around the Sun.
Divide GM☉ by the distance in metres.
Take the square root, then divide by 1,000.
questions.onCorrect: 29.8 km/s. The same circular-speed formula works around the Sun with the Sun's GM.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in metres per second. Divide by 1,000 for km/s.

questions.prompt: Tidal stretching falls as the cube of distance. If the Moon were at half its present distance, by what factor would its tides grow?
hints: A tide is a difference in pull across Earth.
That difference scales as one over distance cubed.
Cube the factor of 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tide ∝ 1/d³, so halving d multiplies the tide by 2³ = 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. A tide is a difference in pull, which scales as 1/d³, so half the distance gives 2³.

misconceptions.feedback: That squares the factor, as for the pull itself. A tide is a difference in pull, which follows the cube.
That follows 1/d. The difference in pull falls faster, as 1/d³.

questions.prompt: The Moon has GM = 4.90 × 10¹² m³/s² and radius 1,737 km. Find the escape speed from its surface in km/s, to two decimal places.
hints: Escape speed is √(2GM/R).
Convert the radius to metres.
Compute the square root and convert to km/s.
questions.onCorrect: 2.38 km/s. Escape speed is √(2GM/R) with the radius in metres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the circular speed at the surface. The escape speed is larger, with a 2 under the root.

questions.prompt: Why are the tides largest around new moon and full moon?
hints: Think about where the Sun lies relative to the Earth–Moon line at those phases.

acceptedIdeas: The Sun's and the Moon's tidal stretches line up and add
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At new and full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon are in line, so the solar tide (0.46 of the lunar tide) adds to the Moon's: spring tides. At the quarters they partly cancel: neap tides.

choices.label: The Sun's and the Moon's tidal stretches line up and add
The Moon is always closest to Earth at those phases
Earth spins faster at those phases

questions.onCorrect: At new and full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon line up, so the two tidal stretches add.

misconceptions.feedback: The Moon's distance varies over the month, but not in step with the phase.
Earth's spin does not change with the Moon's phase. Look at how the Sun and Moon line up.

questions.prompt: A probe moves from 1 AU to 2 AU from the Sun. What fraction of the solar flux it received at 1 AU does it now receive?

Doubling d multiplies that area by 2².
Take the reciprocal of 2².

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Flux ∝ 1/d², so it falls to 1/2² = 1/4 = 0.25 of its value at 1 AU.

questions.onCorrect: 0.25. Flux follows 1/d², so doubling the distance divides the flux by four.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves the flux. It follows the inverse square, so the 2 is squared.

questions.prompt: The Sun's luminosity is 3.828 × 10²⁶ W. Find the flux at 1 AU = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, in W/m², to the nearest whole number.
hints: Use F = L/(4πd²).
Square the distance in metres, then multiply by 4π.
Divide the luminosity by that area.

questions.prompt: Proxima Centauri's parallax is 0.768 arcseconds. Find its distance in parsecs, to two decimal places.

questions.prompt: Star A is 100 times as luminous as star B, yet they appear equally bright. How many times farther away than B is A?
hints: Flux is proportional to L/d².
Keep the flux fixed while L grows a hundredfold.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal flux needs L/d² equal, so d grows as √L: √100 = 10 times farther.

questions.prompt: A star's parallax is 0.05 arcseconds. Find its distance in light-years, to one decimal place, using 1 pc = 3.26 ly.

questions.prompt: What unit of distance is defined as the distance at which a star shows a parallax of one arcsecond?

questions.prompt: Using Wien's law λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T, find the peak wavelength of the Sun (T = 5,772 K) in nanometres, to the nearest whole number.

questions.prompt: A star's spectrum peaks at 290 nm. Find its surface temperature in kelvin, to the nearest hundred.
hints: Rearrange Wien's law for T.
Write the peak wavelength in metres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 2.90 × 10⁻⁷ = 9,993 K, which is 10,000 K to the nearest hundred.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen line with laboratory wavelength 656.28 nm is observed at 662.84 nm. Using v = cΔλ/λ with c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s, find the radial velocity in km/s, to the nearest ten (positive means receding).

Multiply by the speed of light in km/s.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Δλ = 6.56 nm; v = 3.00 × 10⁵ × 6.56/656.28 = 2,999 km/s, which is 3,000 km/s to the nearest ten, receding.

questions.prompt: A star approaches at 150 km/s. Find the shift of its 500.00 nm line in nanometres, with redshift positive and blueshift negative, to three decimal places. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s.

Multiply 500 by −150, then divide by 300,000.

questions.prompt: Betelgeuse looks orange-red and Rigel looks blue-white. What does the difference tell you?

Betelgeuse is moving away from us much faster than Rigel

questions.prompt: A red dwarf has a surface temperature of 3,000 K. Find its peak wavelength in nanometres, to the nearest whole number.

questions.prompt: A star has the Sun's radius but twice the Sun's surface temperature. How many times the Sun's luminosity does it emit?

questions.prompt: A red supergiant has a surface temperature of 3,600 K and a radius of 760 R☉. With T☉ = 5,772 K, find its luminosity in solar units, to the nearest thousand.

questions.prompt: Two stars have the same surface temperature, but one is far more luminous. Which property of the luminous star must be larger? Answer in one word.

questions.prompt: A star twice the Sun's radius has a luminosity of 4 L☉. Taking T☉ = 5,772 K, find its surface temperature in kelvin.

questions.prompt: Main-sequence lifetime scales as t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, with M in solar masses. Find the lifetime of a 4 M☉ star in millions of years, to one decimal place.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4⁻²·⁵ = 1/32, so t = 10 billion/32 = 0.3125 billion years = 312.5 million years.

questions.prompt: Main-sequence luminosity scales roughly as L ∝ M³·⁵. How many times the Sun's luminosity does a 2 M☉ star have? Give one decimal place.
hints: Raise the mass ratio to the power 3.5.
Split 2³·⁵ into 2³ × 2⁰·⁵.
Multiply 8 by √2.

questions.prompt: The Andromeda galaxy is about 0.78 Mpc away, and 1 Mpc = 3.26 million light-years. How long ago, in millions of years, did the light we see from it set out? Give one decimal place.

questions.prompt: Using 1/H₀ = 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀ (H₀ in km/s per Mpc), find 1/H₀ for H₀ = 50, in billions of years, to one decimal place.
